facts.name: Zinnia
facts.color: Many colors, even lime-green flowers (orange-red shown)
facts.moisture: Average, well drained; takes heat and dry spells
facts.notes: Bright, daisy-like flowers in almost every color from midsummer until frost, and a favorite cut flower that butterflies visit. An annual: plant it after the last frost in late May. Snip off faded flowers to keep it blooming, and give it room for air to keep powdery mildew down.

sources.title: MIgardener (Michigan seed company): Cherry Queen Zinnia
sources.note: Zinnia elegans seed sold by a Michigan company (grown in Michigan, store in St. Clair, MI); full sun, up to about 30 inches, blooms summer to frost.

sources.title: MSU Extension: Growing zinnias in your flower garden
sources.note: Zinnias are easy annuals for Michigan gardens: full sun and well-drained soil; deadhead them to keep them blooming from early summer to frost.

sources.title: Wisconsin Horticulture (UW–Madison Extension): Zinnias
sources.note: Sow or set out plants after the last spring frost once the soil warms. Heights run from about 6 inches to 3 to 4 feet by variety; colors include pink, red, orange, yellow, white, lilac, purple and lime green. Resistant to deer; space for air to cut powdery mildew.

sources.title: Rutgers NJAES: Landscape Plants Rated by Deer Resistance
sources.note: Zinnia is rated B, seldom severely damaged.

sources.title: ASPCA: Zinnia
sources.note: Non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

sources.title: Gardenia: Zinnia Flowers, a must-have for every garden
sources.note: Can't take frost: sow after the last frost. Thin compact types to 6 to 8 inches apart and tall types to 12 to 18 inches; plants grow 1 to 4 feet tall.

companions.why: Dahlias make a striking backdrop or companion to zinnias.

sources.title: Gardenia: Zinnia Flowers, a must-have for every garden

companions.why: Salvia goes well with zinnias and draws pollinators.
